book: 277 - Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink

chapters.relation: Porn journalist Gram Ponante's foreword riffs on Plato's Allegory of the Cave, casting porn as the shadows on the cave wall and the viewer as both prisoner and fire. He argues that unlike the manipulated prisoners, the porn viewer actively projects meaning onto a deliberately thin surface — forgiving porn its fake 'MILF' and 'schoolgirl' labels because the images 'become what we want them to be.' Porn is 'a cave to be filled in,' and adding plot or realism only breaks the fantasy by making the images less available for projection.

Dylan Ryder (a working porn star) and Dave Monroe argue that being a porn performer does not necessarily lower the prudential quality of one's life, against the common-sense view (fed by films like Boogie Nights) that porn stars are damaged, coerced, or degraded. They reject Aristotle's claim that virtue is necessary for eudaimonia and, citing Kant's deontology and utilitarianism as theories that sever welfare from morality, distinguish moral value from subjective wellbeing. Deploying the 'Happy Slave' thought experiment and Ron Amundson's disability-welfare research, they contend outsiders' pity reflects social stigma, not the performer's own first-personal welfare judgment.

Andrew Aberdein traces the historical 'interpenetration' of philosophy and pornography — from the French book trade's 'livres philosophiques' and Diderot, d'Argens's Thérèse philosophe, and Sade, back through Aretino's courtesan dialogues to Plato's Symposium (the root of 'platonic love'). He dwells on the medieval 'Lay of Aristotle,' where Phyllis rides Aristotle like a horse, using the image to stage two readings: Aristotle's, that nature (and woman) must submit to the golden mean of reason, versus Phyllis's, that nature cannot. He closes with a paradox aimed at MacKinnon-style subordination arguments: if John Norman's Gor novels show philosophy is less persuasive than porn, then any persuasive argument for censorship must have a false conclusion.

Evolutionary psychologists Anne Gordon and Shane Kraus coin 'porngasm' and, via a survey of 264 undergraduates, argue that watching porn may make men bad lovers because porn caters to male short-term mating psychology and misrepresents female orgasm (which they estimate is 80–95% faked on screen). Men more than women infer that female porn stars genuinely enjoy the sex, and more viewing predicts stronger such belief. They explain the male bias through the correspondence bias (reading moans as real arousal despite the filming situation) and Haselton and Buss's error-management theory, whereby men systematically over-infer women's sexual interest.

Theodore Bach argues that consuming porn co-opts the mind-reading 'simulation heuristic' (the same process behind the Mr. Tees airport puzzle), so that a viewer like 'Max' watching Naughty Office simulates being the boss rather than objectively watching. This explains porn's popularity, the money shot (a prop that keeps the viewer inside the off-line simulation), and why heterosexual men watch penises — they simulate their own. Invoking Nozick's experience machine and extending MacKinnon's critique via simulation and motor-imagery research, Bach warns that simulating aggressive, degrading acts toward women may transfer those dispositions into the real world.

Casey McKittrick accounts for gay 'bareback' pornography — the erotic celebration of condomless anal sex and visible semen exchange (the reinsertion shot, gangbang formats like Dawson's 50-Load Weekend). He situates it against the pathologizing of homosexuality, citing Foucault's History of Sexuality on the Victorian 'invention' of the homosexual and Lee Edelman on queer sexuality as outside reproductive futurity. Drawing on Freud's account of loss and the death drive (eros and thanatos), he reads semen as the 'lost object' — 'brothers' milk' — and bareback video as a fantasy screen restoring intimacy severed by AIDS, animating the struggle between the erotic and the lethal.

Tait Szabo defends the guiltless consumption of pornography using Mill's Harm Principle from On Liberty: harmless conduct, even if deemed immoral, should not be censored. Classifying porn into erotica, sexist, dominance, and violent types (excluding child porn and snuff as clearly prohibitable), he rebuts the arguments that porn is prostitution (citing California v. Freeman), that loveless sex is wrong, that porn non-rationally causes or conditions violence against women, and the anti-porn feminist claim that it eroticizes patriarchal subordination. Each argument, he holds, either lacks causal evidence or would equally condemn romance novels, sexist jokes, and Cinderella — so under Mill, censorship is unjustified.

Fiona Woollard asks whether Zach's solo use of pornography (while partner Kelly is out) counts as cheating on their monogamous relationship. Drawing on her account of monogamy as restricting sexual intercourse to loving relationships, she argues that masturbation to porn is not sexual intercourse — there is no interaction with 'Jenna' — and that fantasizing about loveless sex is not the same as having it, so it need not undermine the significance of lovemaking; indeed masturbation aids healthy sexual self-exploration. She concedes, however, that porn which eroticizes the degradation of women (per Dworkin and MacKinnon, and Alice Walker's story 'Porn') can betray a loving relationship by revealing objectifying attitudes.

Darci Doll treats celebrity sex tapes (Pamela Anderson/Tommy Lee, Paris Hilton, Kim Kardashian, Colin Farrell) as a cautionary tale about privately recorded porn. She argues taping is defensible only with informed adult consent and agreed terms of distribution, then analyzes the appeal — celebrity obsession, voyeurism, and the fantasy of 'having sex with' a star — and the motives for release, including career boosts. Against these she sets the risks of theft, accident, and betrayal by a jilted ex, plus the 'sexting' problem among minors, concluding that because release is essentially irreversible, a sexually positive culture must protect trust rather than assume amateur tapes are safe from a market.

Jacob Held argues that US obscenity and anti-pornography law fails for indeterminacy. Tracing Roth v. United States (Brennan's 'prurient interest' standard) and Miller v. California's three-part 'serious value' test, he shows judges must act as aesthetes (Justice Stewart's 'I know it when I see it'; Scalia's doubt about objective artistic value), so the law gives no fair notice and lacks the form a rule of law requires. He then turns to MacKinnon and Dworkin's Indianapolis civil-rights ordinance defining porn as the 'subordination of women,' struck down in American Booksellers v. Hudnut, arguing its vague 'subordinating' criterion — read through Dworkin's jaded view of sex — would sweep in nearly all explicit material, per Douglas that 'censors are propelled by their own neuroses.'

Mimi Marinucci asks 'what's wrong with porn?' and, rejecting both the Dworkin-MacKinnon censorship route and Strossen's pure free-speech reply, uses Audre Lorde's notion of the erotic as power and the personal test 'it feels right to me' as an entering wedge. She examines 'feminist porn,' resisting its easy equation with lesbian or couples porn, and contrasts it with 'fuck machine porn' (e.g., machines named Annihilator, Predator), which feels wrong to her not for size or domination but because mainstream porn fixates on decontextualized acts and the money shot. Citing Irigaray on women's diffuse, non-localized sexuality, she argues women want more richly contextualized representations than porn typically offers.

holes.name: Audre Lorde
holes.what: Black lesbian feminist poet-theorist whose essay 'Uses of the Erotic: The Erotic as Power' theorizes the erotic as a deep source of female self-knowledge and power distinct from pornography.
holes.why: Chapter 10 (ch24) builds its whole positive account of what 'feels right' in porn on Lorde's erotic-as-power, but no Lorde slug exists in the taxonomy.

holes.name: The Erotic as Power
holes.what: Lorde's idea that the erotic is a disciplined internal resource and a form of empowering knowledge, sharply opposed to the sensation-without-feeling of pornography.
holes.why: Marinucci's argument turns on distinguishing empowering erotic experience from oppressive porn, a concept the taxonomy has no slug for (objectification and mackinnon-dominance capture only the critique side).

holes.name: Denis Diderot
holes.what: French Enlightenment philosophe and Encyclopédie editor who also wrote erotic-philosophical fiction (Les Bijoux indiscrets, Supplément au voyage de Bougainville).
holes.why: Aberdein's central case for the philosophy/pornography synthesis rests on Diderot as a canonical Enlightenment philosopher writing porn, but the taxonomy lists no Diderot slug.
